misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps the e before -ing or adds -ed after e
misconceptions.description: Writes bakeing or smileed: the final e is kept before a vowel ending.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the rule: e goes away when -ing comes to stay; build the word on a strip and fold the e under.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Does not double after a short vowel
misconceptions.description: Writes claping or hoping for hopping: the consonant after a short vowel is not doubled, which can make another word.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Clap the vowel: short vowel, one consonant, double it; compare hoping and hopping.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps y after a consonant
misconceptions.description: Writes flys or cryed: the y after a consonant is not changed to i.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at the letter before y: a consonant means change y to i, then add es or ed.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds -s where -es is needed
misconceptions.description: Writes catchs or washs: -s is added after ch, sh, s or x, where the word needs -es.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word aloud: if adding the ending makes an extra beat, write -es.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Matches words by their letters, not their sound
misconceptions.description: Picks the word that looks the same instead of the one that sounds the same: ticks on as rhyming with won, or puts heard with head.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say both words aloud and listen to the middle sound before choosing; cover the letters and listen.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Says unusual letters with their usual sound
misconceptions.description: Reads letters with their most common sound in a word where they say another: thinks month does not share the o of brother, or puts bread with seat.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Collect a family of words where the letters make the unusual sound (bread, head, ready) and read them aloud together.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes the sound-alike word with the other meaning
misconceptions.description: Chooses a word that sounds the same but means something else: here for hear, to for two, their spelt there.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask what the word means in this sentence, then match it to the spelling with that meaning (hear has an ear in it).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up two words that nearly sound alike
misconceptions.description: Chooses a word that sounds or looks nearly the same: quite for quiet, were for where, off for of, then for than.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say both words slowly to hear the difference, and keep a short sentence for each one.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Guesses a word from its first letters
misconceptions.description: Reads the start of the word and picks another word that begins the same: thought or though for through, quit for quiet.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the whole word to the end, then read the sentence again to check it makes sense.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out a part of a long word
misconceptions.description: Joins or reads the parts but drops one: writes diffrent for different, intresting for interesting.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Clap the parts, say each one, and tick it off as it is written.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Guesses a long word from its start and does not check the sentence
misconceptions.description: Picks a word that starts with the same letters but does not make sense: helmet for helicopter, carpet for carrot.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read every part of the word, then read the sentence with it and ask: does it make sense?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up -dge and -ge
misconceptions.description: Writes ge after a short vowel or dge after a long vowel: fuge for fudge, hudge for huge.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Short vowel just before the j sound: dge (badge, hedge). Long vowel or a consonant: ge (huge, large).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Ends a word with j
misconceptions.description: Writes j for the j sound at the end of a word: fudj for fudge, huj for huge.
misconceptions.repair_hint: English words do not end in j; at the end, the j sound is written ge or dge.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up -ck and -k
misconceptions.description: Writes k or c after a short vowel, or ck after a consonant: duk for duck, tiket for ticket, milck for milk.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Short vowel just before the k sound: ck (duck, sock). After a consonant: k (milk, desk).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses c where k is needed at the start, or k where c is
misconceptions.description: Writes c before e, i or y, or k before a, o or u: cite for kite, kup for cup.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Before e, i or y the k sound is written k (kite, keep); before a, o, u or a consonant it is c (cup, cold).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Drops the e before a suffix that starts with a consonant
misconceptions.description: Takes the final e off the root when the suffix does not start with a vowel: carless for careless, replacment for replacement.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Drop the e only before a vowel suffix such as -ing; -less, -ness and -ment keep it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Drops a letter where the root and the suffix meet
misconceptions.description: Writes one letter where the root ends and the suffix begins with the same letter: openess for openness.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the whole root, then the whole suffix: open + ness keeps both n's.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Matches a prefix or suffix to the wrong meaning
misconceptions.description: Matches re- with not, or -less with being: pairs inactive with appear again, or painless with being sad.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Learn one meaning for each: re- again, in- not, -less without, -ness being, and test the word in a sentence.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells the suffix short or wrong
misconceptions.description: Writes the suffix with a letter missing or changed: kindnes for kindness, careles for careless, enjoymant for enjoyment.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Practise -ness, -less and -ment as whole chunks: each ending is always spelt the same.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes to where too is needed
misconceptions.description: Uses to for too when the meaning is also or more than enough: It is to hot. Can I come to?
misconceptions.repair_hint: Too means also or too much, and it has too many o's.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up right and write
misconceptions.description: Writes right for putting words on paper, or write for correct or a direction: right your name, turn write.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write starts with a silent w, like the w on a worksheet you write on.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Changes a word that was already right
misconceptions.description: While fixing the mistakes, also changes a correct word: changes went to the beach into went too the beach.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read each word and ask what it means before changing it; leave a word that already fits.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes a compound word as two words
misconceptions.description: Leaves a space or puts a hyphen between the two parts: bed room, tea-pot, thunder storm.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A compound word is one word: join the two parts with no gap.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Drops a letter from a part of a compound word
misconceptions.description: Spells one of the joined words short: footbal for football, grandaughter for granddaughter.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Spell the first word in full, then the second word in full, and check where they meet.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells a tricky word the way it sounds
misconceptions.description: Writes the letters heard in the word, not its real spelling: frend for friend, becos for because, Wensday for Wednesday.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use a memory trick or say it as it is spelt (Wed-nes-day; I am your friend to the end), then look, cover, write, check.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out a silent letter
misconceptions.description: Leaves out a letter that is not heard: lisen for listen, nife for knife.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word as it is spelt, with the silent letter (lis-ten), and underline that letter when practising.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Splits a long word in the wrong place
misconceptions.description: Writes pain as the root of repaint, or splits disagreement as di + sag + reement: the cut does not follow the prefix, root and suffix.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the prefix first, then the suffix, and check that what is left is a word you know.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves a prefix or suffix on the root
misconceptions.description: Writes helpful as the root of unhelpful, or believable for unbelievable: one added part is still on the root.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Take off every added part, front and back, until only the smallest word is left.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Does not put back the root's changed letter
misconceptions.description: Writes happi as the root of unhappily, or believ for unbelievable: the y or e that changed is not restored.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask whether what is left is a real word; if not, try putting back an e or changing i to y.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Ignores what the prefix or suffix means
misconceptions.description: Ticks 'full of fear' for fearless, or 'can be replaced easily' for irreplaceable: the meaning of the added part is lost or reversed.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say what each part means (un- not, -less without), then read the sentence again with that meaning.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Always picks the first syllable as the strong one
misconceptions.description: Ticks bal for bal-loon or com for com-pu-ter: the first part is chosen whatever the word.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word with the beat on each part in turn; the one that sounds right is the strong one.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a weak syllable as the strong one
misconceptions.description: Ticks fin for tif-fin or lar for cat-er-pil-lar: a quiet, later part is chosen as the strong beat.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Clap the word and say it loudly on the beat you choose; listen for the part that sounds natural.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives the strong syllable when asked for the weak one
misconceptions.description: Ticks way when asked for the weak part of a-way: the strong part is given instead of the quiet one.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the strong part first, then choose a part that is not it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps one stress for a noun and a verb spelt the same
misconceptions.description: Ticks re for re-cord in 'We will record a song': the noun's stress is used for the verb, or the other way round.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask whether the word names a thing or an action; things often take the beat first, actions later.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a word that sounds right but means something else
misconceptions.description: Writes here for hear, or peace for piece: the word sounds the same but has the other meaning.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence and ask what the word must mean; link it to a word you know (hear has ear).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Swaps two near-alike words
misconceptions.description: Writes quite for quiet, then for than, or desert for dessert: the near-alike word with the other meaning is chosen.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say both words slowly to hear the difference, and keep a meaning clue for each (dessert has two s for sweet stuff).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a word with nearly the same letters
misconceptions.description: Writes expect for except, or quit for quiet: a word that looks almost the same is chosen.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read each letter of the word you chose, then read the sentence with it to check it makes sense.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the silent letter
misconceptions.description: Writes nit for knit, rist for wrist or colum for column: the letter that is not said is left out.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word as it is spelt (k-nit, colum-n) to remember the silent letter, then say it normally.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells the short u sound with u every time
misconceptions.description: Writes munth for month, gluv for glove or tuch for touch: the o or ou spelling is replaced with u.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Keep a list of o and ou words for the short u sound (month, money, touch) and learn them as a family.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells the vowel after w as it sounds
misconceptions.description: Writes wosh for wash, werm for worm or wurld for world: the vowel is spelt by its sound, not as wa, war or wor.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Learn the w families: wa says o in wash, war says or in warm, wor says ur in worm.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Changes y to ies after a vowel
misconceptions.description: Writes monkies for monkeys or donkies for donkeys: y is changed even though a vowel comes before it.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at the letter before y: a vowel means keep the y and add -s; a consonant means change to -ies.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps the f in the plural
misconceptions.description: Writes leafs, shelfs or calfs: the f or fe is not changed to -ves.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the plural aloud: if you hear a v sound, change the f or fe to v and add -es.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds only -s to a word ending in o that needs -es
misconceptions.description: Writes potatos, tomatos or heros: -s is added where the plural takes -es.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Learn the -oes words as a group: potatoes, tomatoes, heroes, echoes.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Misspells the prefix
misconceptions.description: Writes tranport for transport or priheat for preheat: a letter of trans- or pre- is lost, added or changed.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the prefix first, check it letter by letter, then add the root without changing either.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells the suffix as it sounds
misconceptions.description: Writes collecshun for collection or poisonus for poisonous: -ion or -ous is spelt by its sound.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Remember that the shun sound at the end is usually spelt -tion, and the us sound is spelt -ous.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses -ion where -ation is needed, or the other way
misconceptions.description: Writes predictation for prediction or admirion for admiration: the wrong one of -ion and -ation is added.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the new word aloud and listen for the extra 'ay' sound: if you hear it, use -ation.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses there or they're for 'belonging to them'
misconceptions.description: Writes 'the twins packed there tiffin boxes': there or they're where the word must show the thing belongs to them.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask 'whose is it?'. If the answer is 'theirs', write their: it has 'heir' inside, and an heir owns things.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses their or they're for a place or 'there is'
misconceptions.description: Writes 'the auto-rickshaw is over their' or 'Their is a mango tree': their or they're for a place or for 'there is / there are'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: There has 'here' inside it: here and there are both places. 'There is' and 'there are' use the same word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses their or there for 'they are'
misconceptions.description: Writes 'their going to the market' or 'there ready': their or there where the sentence means 'they are'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the sentence with 'they are' in the gap. If it still makes sense, write they're, with the apostrophe for the missing a.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up your and you're
misconceptions.description: Writes 'your going to get wet' for you are, or 'put you're shoes by the door' for belonging to you.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read it with 'you are'. If that makes sense, write you're; if the thing belongs to you, write your.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes the sound instead of the -ough string
misconceptions.description: Writes enuff for enough, coff for cough, doe for dough or drout for drought: the sound is spelt, not the letter string.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Keep a word list for each sound of -ough. Look, say the sound, cover, write, check.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes -augh for -ough
misconceptions.description: Writes baught for bought or thaught for thought: the -augh of caught and taught is used where the word needs -ough.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Most 'or' words ending in t are -ought (bought, brought, fought, thought); learn caught, taught and daughter as the -augh group.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes the sound instead of the -ear string
misconceptions.description: Writes yeer for year, bair for bear or erth for earth: the sound is spelt, not the ear letter string.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Sort ear words by sound (hear, bear, learn, heart) and practise one group at a time.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Sorts by the letters, not by the sound
misconceptions.description: Puts dough with rough, or heart with hear, in a sort by sound: the words look alike, so they are put in one group.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say each word aloud before sorting it. The letters are the same in every word; only the sound decides the group.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a word that follows the rule as the odd one out
misconceptions.description: Ticks ladies, not monkeys, as the word that breaks the y to ies pattern: the choice goes by meaning or length, not by the spelling pattern.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the root beside each word (lady, monkey) and look at the letters that changed. The odd one changed in a different way.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses a rule on a word it does not fit
misconceptions.description: Writes vallies for valleys or monkies for monkeys: the y to ies rule is used after a vowel, where only -s is added.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Every rule has a 'when'. Check the letter before the y (or the e, or the last consonant) before using it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Spells a tricky word as it sounds
misconceptions.description: Writes becos for because, frend for friend, anser for answer or rythm for rhythm: the letters that are not heard are left out.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Use a memory trick for the hidden letters (big elephants can always understand small elephants) and look, cover, write, check.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Drops a part of the word that is not said clearly
misconceptions.description: Writes libary for library, Wensday for Wednesday, vegtable for vegetable or intresting for interesting.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word in its parts, slowly and clearly (Wed-nes-day, li-brar-y), then write one part at a time.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Swaps ie and ei
misconceptions.description: Writes beleive for believe or freind for friend: the i and e are in the wrong order.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the small word inside: 'a lie' in believe, 'end' in friend (a friend to the end).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Doubles the wrong letter, or misses a double
misconceptions.description: Writes neccessary for necessary or tommorow for tomorrow: a letter is doubled that should not be, or one letter of a pair is left out.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Learn the double letters with a trick: necessary has one collar and two sleeves (one c, two s).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Judges a word family by the look, not the meaning
misconceptions.description: Puts carrot in the care family or helmet with help, or leaves caring out of the family because the e has gone.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask what each word means. A family shares a root and a meaning, not only a few letters.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Changes the root's spelling when adding to it
misconceptions.description: Writes musition for musician, electrisity for electricity or conection for connection: the root is spelt by its new sound.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the root word first and write it unchanged (music, electric, connect), then add the ending.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives the wrong meaning for a root
misconceptions.description: Says tele means sound in telephone, television and telescope, or that act means telling a story.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put the family side by side and ask what every word has in common; test the meaning on each word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Stops at the first letter when words share it
misconceptions.description: Leaves words that start with the same letter in the order they were printed, e.g. writes cricket before chess.
misconceptions.repair_hint: When two words start with the same letter, cover it and compare the next letter.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts a letter in the wrong place in the alphabet
misconceptions.description: Orders by first letter but slips in the alphabet, e.g. writes mango before kite because m is thought to come before k.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the alphabet aloud with a printed strip and point to each first letter.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up two words of the same topic
misconceptions.description: Picks a topic word with a different meaning, e.g. writes prey for an owl that hunts, or condensation for water rising as vapour.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say what each topic word means in your own words, then check which meaning the sentence needs.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses a word from another topic
misconceptions.description: Picks a word that belongs to a different topic and does not fit, e.g. writes weather for where a frog lives.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: what is this sentence about? Choose a word from that topic.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses a vague everyday word instead of the topic word
misconceptions.description: Writes a general word where the topic has its own word, e.g. writes stuff instead of ingredients.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Keep a topic word list and swap the everyday word for the exact one.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Guesses a meaning that ignores the clue
misconceptions.description: Picks a meaning that could fit the spot in the sentence but not its clue, e.g. says drenched means very hungry when water dripped from his hair.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Underline the clue words first, then choose the meaning that agrees with them.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives the meaning of a nearby word
misconceptions.description: Gives a meaning taken from another word close by, e.g. says drenched means raining hard because rain is in the sentence.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put your finger on the new word and ask what that one word tells us.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes the meaning of a word that looks or sounds the same
misconceptions.description: Uses the meaning of a look-alike word or another sense of it, e.g. says minute means sixty seconds when the frogs are tiny.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence with your meaning in place: does it still make sense?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks the opposite instead of a synonym
misconceptions.description: Chooses a word that means the opposite, e.g. ticks tiny for a word that means the same as huge.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put the word back in the sentence: does the sentence still mean the same thing?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a word about the same thing, not the same meaning
misconceptions.description: Chooses a word that goes with the topic but means something else, e.g. ticks round for a word that means the same as big.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A synonym can swap places with the word and the meaning stays the same; test the swap.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses a synonym for another meaning of the word
misconceptions.description: Swaps good for a word that fits a different use of good, e.g. writes delicious medicine for good medicine.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask what good means in this sentence before you choose: tasty, kind, well-behaved or helpful?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks the naming word, not the describing word
misconceptions.description: Underlines the noun the adjective describes, e.g. underlines mango in a juicy mango.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the thing first, then ask: what word tells me what it is like?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks the doing word as a describing word
misconceptions.description: Underlines the verb, e.g. underlines kicked in the tall boy kicked the muddy football.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A describing word sits next to a thing, not an action: try putting it in front of a noun.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Finds some describing words but misses others
misconceptions.description: Underlines only the first describing word of a group, e.g. marks soft but not green in a soft green shawl.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read each noun phrase slowly and touch every word in front of the noun.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds a dull word that makes no picture
misconceptions.description: Adds a describing word that tells the reader nothing new, e.g. writes a nice river or a good bird.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Close your eyes and picture it: what colour, size, sound or feel can you see? Write that word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks an action word as a sound word
misconceptions.description: Underlines a word for a movement that makes no sound of its own, e.g. underlines jumped in Splash! Arjun jumped into the puddle.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the word aloud: does it sound like the noise? If not, it is not a sound word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks a word that names a sound but does not copy it
misconceptions.description: Underlines a word about sound or hearing, e.g. thunder, noise or heard, instead of the word that copies the sound, such as boom.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A sound word copies the noise itself; ask: could I make this noise by saying the word?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a sound word that does not match the thing
misconceptions.description: Picks a sound word for a different thing, e.g. writes quack for a cow or crashed for a candle flame.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Picture the thing making its noise, then choose the word that sounds like that noise.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up when openers and where openers
misconceptions.description: Sorts a time opener as a place, or a place as a time, e.g. puts On Sunday with the where openers because it starts with On.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask the question: does it answer when? or where? Not which little word it starts with.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up how openers with when or where
misconceptions.description: Sorts a how opener as a time or place, e.g. puts Quietly with the when openers, or ticks On Monday for how.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A how opener tells the way something is done; try saying it in what way? before it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses an opener that does not link to the sentence before
misconceptions.description: Picks an opener that breaks the order of events, e.g. Yesterday in the middle of one day's story, or Last year after packing bags for today.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence before, then ask: what happened next, and where or when?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the comma after the opener
misconceptions.description: Writes the opener and runs straight on, e.g. After lunch we drew a rangoli with no comma after lunch.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Pause after the opener when you read it aloud; put a comma where you pause.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a speech verb that does not match how it is said
misconceptions.description: Picks a speech verb that goes against the clues, e.g. shouted for a baby who is asleep, or whispered for Fire! Get out now!
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for the clues: the marks, the words spoken and how the speaker feels. Then choose.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a verb that is not a way of speaking
misconceptions.description: Puts an action verb where the speech verb goes, e.g. writes ran in "The baby is asleep," ran Mum.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: is this a way to use your voice? If not, it cannot follow the spoken words.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads the wrong feeling from a speech verb
misconceptions.description: Says the speech verb shows a feeling it does not, e.g. says snapped shows Ananya was frightened.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Act out the verb: say the words that way and notice how you feel.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Orders by the first letter only
misconceptions.description: When words share their first letters, leaves them in the printed order: writes shop, shell, shut, ship for shell, ship, shop, shut.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the letters that match and compare the first letter that is different.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Stops at the third letter when the fourth is needed
misconceptions.description: Sorts by the third letter but leaves words that match for three letters in printed order: puts monsoon before money.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Keep going letter by letter until two words differ, even at the fourth or fifth letter.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts a short word after the longer word it starts
misconceptions.description: Writes peach before pea, or plane before plan, as if the longer word comes first.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Nothing comes before something: when one word runs out of letters first, it goes first.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Misreads the guide words of a dictionary page
misconceptions.description: Picks chair or cherry for the page headed chalk and cheese because they begin with ch.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Check the word comes after the first guide word AND before the second one.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses an everyday word where the topic word is needed
misconceptions.description: Writes things or stuff in a science sentence instead of clouds or vessels.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: what would the expert in this topic call it? Look back at the topic word list.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a topic word with a close but wrong meaning
misconceptions.description: Writes evaporation for condensation, axis for orbit, or magma for lava.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say what each topic word means in a few plain words, then choose the one that matches the sentence exactly.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives the opposite meaning
misconceptions.description: Writes simple for baffling or calm for turbulent, missing a clue such as but or not.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for but, so and not: they tell you whether the new word agrees with the clue or turns it round.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a word that fits the scene, not the new word
misconceptions.description: Picks colourful for an enormous rangoli or muddy for a turbulent river: true of the scene, but not the meaning.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put your word in place of the new word: the sentence must say the same thing as before.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives a synonym of the wrong word class
misconceptions.description: Writes dryness for arid or roughly for turbulent: the meaning is close, but the word does not fit the sentence.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Swap your word into the sentence and read it aloud: it must fit where the new word was.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Replaces an overused word with another plain one
misconceptions.description: Changes a nice day to a good day, or a lot of to lots of: the new word is just as tired.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask what exactly was nice about it, then choose a word that says that.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a strong word that changes the meaning
misconceptions.description: Replaces a nice day with a sleepy day, or a lot of grapes with a few grapes.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Check the new word still tells the truth about what happened in the text.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies plain words when asked for strong ones
misconceptions.description: When asked for the writer's strong words, copies ordinary words such as front, got or day.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A strong word gives a clear picture or sound; test it by asking what you see or hear.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Rewrites the sentence but loses its meaning
misconceptions.description: Rewrites 'Zoya got her umbrella' as 'Zoya lost her umbrella' or leaves out part of the sentence.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the old and new sentences one after the other: the same thing must happen in both.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Orders from strongest to weakest
misconceptions.description: Writes furious, angry, annoyed when asked for weakest to strongest.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Start with the gentlest word, the one you would use for the smallest feeling.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gets the ends right but swaps the middle words
misconceptions.description: Writes cool, cold, chilly, freezing: the first and last are right, the middle pair is swapped.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put each middle word into the same sentence and ask which is a little stronger.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a word too strong for the sentence
misconceptions.description: Writes furious when the sentence says only a little upset, or heavy for a shower of a few drops.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the clue words (only, a little, absolutely) that say how strong the word must be.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a word too weak for the sentence
misconceptions.description: Writes cool for a lassi so cold it hurts, or uneasy for someone who screamed and ran away.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at what happened next in the sentence: does your word match how big it was?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Calls any sentence with like a simile
misconceptions.description: Picks 'Aman likes the bangle stall best' as a simile because it has the word like in it.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A simile compares two different things: check that something is said to be like something else.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes alliteration up with rhyme or a simile
misconceptions.description: Picks 'flying high in the sky' (a rhyme) or 'as fresh as a mint leaf' (a simile) as alliteration.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the first sound of each word aloud: alliteration is the same first sound, close together.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Underlines only part of a simile or alliteration
misconceptions.description: Underlines just cheetah instead of as fast as a cheetah, or only sparrows in seven small sparrows sat.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Underline every word of the comparison, from like or the first as to the thing compared.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads a simile as if it were really true
misconceptions.description: Says the rain really was made of metal needles, or that Grandpa's fingers are made of wood.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: in what way are the two things alike? Name that one shared quality.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Names the figure but does not explain it
misconceptions.description: Writes 'it is a simile' and stops, without saying what picture or sound it gives the reader.
misconceptions.repair_hint: After naming it, finish the sentence 'It makes me picture…' or 'It sounds like…'.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes a comparison that does not fit
misconceptions.description: Writes as cold as toast, or a tired old dog as fast as a rocket: the two things are not alike in the way needed.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Name the quality first (cold, slow, noisy), then think of something that is famous for it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes a comparison without like or as
misconceptions.description: Writes 'the kite was a bird' or just adds an adjective, 'the red kite', instead of a simile.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A simile needs like or as … as to join the two things: check one is there.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Alliteration that breaks its sound
misconceptions.description: Writes 'busy buzzing fly' or 'silly parrot sang': one word in the run starts with a different sound.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the phrase aloud and tap each first sound: every tap must be the same.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps the plain verb
misconceptions.description: Chooses ate, said, took or walked again when asked for a stronger verb.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: how exactly did it happen? Choose the verb that shows how.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a strong verb that does not fit the scene
misconceptions.description: Chooses stomped for a thief who must not wake anyone, or skipped for a tired runner.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for the clue about mood or speed in the sentence; the verb must agree with it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds an adverb instead of changing the verb
misconceptions.description: Writes 'walked very quietly' instead of choosing one strong verb such as crept.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Try to say it all in one verb: crept already means walked quietly.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Says what the verb means but not what it adds
misconceptions.description: Writes 'hammered means hit' without saying what the reader hears or pictures.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Finish the sentence 'This verb makes me picture…' or 'This verb makes me hear…'.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes a short form with a word that sounds the same
misconceptions.description: Writes were for we're, its for it's or their for they're, or reads whose as who is.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the two full words in the sentence: if they're makes sense as they are, it needs the apostrophe.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads a short form as the wrong two words
misconceptions.description: Says they've stands for they are, or ticks it's for is not: the letters before the apostrophe are not read.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the end of the short form, read the first word, then say which word the end letters come from.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Names the wrong missing letter
misconceptions.description: Says the apostrophe in shouldn't stands for u or d, when the letter left out is the o of not.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the two full words above the short form and cross out the letters that went: the apostrophe sits on them.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves the apostrophe out of a short form
misconceptions.description: Writes isnt, theyll or Im: the letters are shortened but no apostrophe shows where they went.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Every time letters are left out, the apostrophe takes their seat; point to the gap before writing.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts the apostrophe where the two words join
misconceptions.description: Writes is'nt, could'nt or did'nt: the apostrophe goes between the two words instead of where the o of not was.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the two words, rub out only the missing letter, and put the apostrophe in exactly that space.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds an apostrophe but keeps every letter
misconceptions.description: Writes we'are, I'am or was'not: an apostrophe is added but no letter is left out.
misconceptions.repair_hint: An apostrophe replaces letters; if nothing is missing, it is two words and needs no apostrophe.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses a full stop for every sentence
misconceptions.description: Writes Where is my water bottle. or Can we play kabaddi after lunch. with a full stop after a question.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence aloud: if your voice asks, it needs a question mark; if it shouts with feeling, an exclamation mark.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Thinks any sentence with a question word is a question
misconceptions.description: Writes I wonder where Dadi kept the sweets? or calls What a beautiful rangoli you made! a question, because of where or what.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: does the sentence want an answer from someone? If not, the question word does not make it a question.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Runs two sentences together
misconceptions.description: Writes The monsoon has come at last can we go out? with one end mark for two sentences and no capital for the second.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read aloud and listen for where the voice stops and starts again; put the end mark there and a capital after it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Names the sentence kind from its end mark only
misconceptions.description: Calls Hold the string tightly! an exclamation because of the exclamation mark, or Is the shop open today? a statement.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at the first words before the mark: a bossy verb first means a command, whatever mark ends it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Calls a command a statement
misconceptions.description: Calls Wash your hands before lunch. a statement because it ends with a full stop.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: is the sentence telling someone to do something? Find the bossy verb at or near the start.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts the narrator's words inside the speech marks
misconceptions.description: Writes "Come and see my kite, said Ria." or underlines The bus is here said Kabir: said and the name are inside.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Act it out: only the words that come out of the character's mouth go inside the marks.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks only part of what is said
misconceptions.description: Underlines I like mango but not lassi, or opens the speech marks and forgets to close them.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find where the speaking starts and where it stops; one mark opens, one mark closes, every spoken word between.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts the end mark outside the closing speech marks
misconceptions.description: Writes "Dinner is ready". or "Where is my cap" asked Rohan? with the full stop or question mark outside.
misconceptions.repair_hint: The spoken words keep their own end mark, tucked inside the closing speech marks.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts speech marks round talk that is only reported
misconceptions.description: Underlines nobody should stand while the bus was moving, which the story only tells us she said.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: are these the exact words the person spoke? Words after said that are reported, not spoken, and get no marks.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes a different kind of sentence from the one asked
misconceptions.description: Asked for a command, writes You mix the curd and sugar., a statement; asked for an exclamation, writes a question.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Before writing, say which kind is asked for and what its first words usually look like.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes a question without turning the words round
misconceptions.description: Writes You like mangoes? or Where you live? keeping statement order and only adding a question mark.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Move the helping verb to the front: You do like becomes Do you like; check the question still sounds right aloud.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Ignores the time word
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Yesterday Aarav plays cricket': the verb does not follow yesterday, tomorrow or every day.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Circle the time word first, then ask: is this before now, now, or after now?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds -ed to an irregular verb
misconceptions.description: Writes catched, rised or finded instead of caught, rose or found.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Keep a list of the irregular verbs met this term and say the past aloud: catch, caught.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts a changed verb after will
misconceptions.description: Writes 'will travelled' or 'will goes': the verb after will is not in its plain form.
misconceptions.repair_hint: After will, use the verb as it is in the dictionary: will go, will travel.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Slips into another tense
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Last Diwali we lit lamps and Dadi makes ladoos': the tense changes for no reason.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the whole piece aloud and check every verb sits in the same time as the first one.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Changes the tense inside speech marks
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Grandpa said, "Next Holi I showed you"': the spoken words are forced into the past to match the story.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Words inside speech marks keep the time of the speaker: what they say about tomorrow stays in the future.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up is and are
misconceptions.description: Writes 'The mangoes is ripe' or 'My sister are in Class 4'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: is the subject one thing or more than one? One takes is, more than one takes are.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses was with we, you, they or a plural
misconceptions.description: Writes 'We was at the festival' or 'The puppies was sleeping'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the pairs aloud: I was, he was, we were, they were, the puppies were.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up has and have
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Arjun and Tara has a coach' or 'The box have a crack'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Two or more people, or I, you, we, they: have. One person or thing: has.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Agrees with the nearest noun, not the subject
misconceptions.description: Writes 'The box of sweets are on the table': the verb follows sweets, not box.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the words starting with of or that; read the subject and verb together: the box is.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a connective with the wrong meaning
misconceptions.description: Writes 'We cannot play because we finish our homework' where unless is needed: the link between the ideas is lost.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the two parts and ask how they are linked: a reason, a condition, a time or a purpose.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks a word that does not join
misconceptions.description: Underlines indoors, quietly or read as the joining word.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A connective joins two parts; cover it and check the sentence falls into two pieces.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Finds only some of the connectives
misconceptions.description: Underlines since but misses until in the same sentence, or spots and and but only.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for every word that starts a new part of the sentence, not just the first.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Joins two sentences with only a comma
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Kiran saved her money, she wanted a bat': no connective links the two parts.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A comma cannot join two sentences on its own; add a connective such as so that or since.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses much with things you can count, or many with things you cannot
misconceptions.description: Writes 'There are much birds' or 'How many milk is left?'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: can I count them one by one? Birds: many. Milk: much.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts the wrong form of the noun after the quantifier
misconceptions.description: Writes 'every children' or 'all visitor' or 'many child': each and every need one, many and all need more than one.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Each and every go with one: every child. Many, several and all go with more than one: many children.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up few and little
misconceptions.description: Writes 'very few water' or 'a little children', or 'a few salt' in a recipe.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Few is for things you count (few birds); little is for things you cannot count (little water).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a quantifier that does not fit the meaning
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Many people stopped' when the passage says the stall was quiet all morning.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence before the gap and decide: a lot, some, or hardly any?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes an adjective for an adverb
misconceptions.description: Underlines hot or noisy as the word that tells how, or writes 'water them gentle'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: An adverb tells more about the verb; ask: how did she stir? Slowly.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks only part of an adverbial phrase
misconceptions.description: Underlines neem tree, or only lunch, instead of the whole phrase under the neem tree or after lunch.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Mark from the small word that starts the phrase (after, under, with) to the end of the idea.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts an adverb in the wrong group
misconceptions.description: Sorts yesterday under where, or outside under when.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask the question for each group: how? when? where? and see which one the word answers.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Thinks only words ending in -ly are adverbs
misconceptions.description: Misses tomorrow, outside or soon, and may mark lovely or friendly because they end in -ly.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Test the word with how, when or where, not by its ending.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds an adverb that does not make the instruction exact
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Water the plants nicely': the reader still does not know how, when or where.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Choose a word or phrase a reader could act on: every evening, with a small can, near the window.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts a comma where a full stop is needed
misconceptions.description: Writes 'The bell rang, we ran to the hall.': two sentences held together by a comma.
misconceptions.repair_hint: If both parts make sense on their own, end the first with a full stop.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses the wrong end mark for a question
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Where is my water bottle.' or puts a question mark after 'Papa wondered whether the buses were running?'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Is someone asking, waiting for an answer? Then use ?. Telling about a question (wondered whether, asked why) ends with a full stop.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Starts a new sentence without a capital letter
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Our cat sleeps on the sofa. she snores softly.'
misconceptions.repair_hint: After every . ? or ! the next word starts with a capital letter.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Ends an exclamation with a full stop
misconceptions.description: Writes 'What a mess it was.' where a strong feeling needs !.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Sentences that begin What a or How and show a strong feeling end with !.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the commas in a list
misconceptions.description: Writes 'We bought mangoes bananas and grapes.' with no comma between the items.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a comma after each item in the list except the last two, which are joined by and.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the comma after an opening phrase
misconceptions.description: Writes 'After the long walk home we drank cold lassi.' with no comma after home.
misconceptions.repair_hint: When a sentence starts with when, where or how something happened, put a comma before the main part.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the comma before or after the name of the person spoken to
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Please pass me the salt Ammi.' or 'Neha could you bring the paints?'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a comma between the name of the person you are talking to and the rest of the sentence.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts commas where they are not needed
misconceptions.description: Writes 'She took, a cap a torch, and a towel.' or 'Nikhil, found frogs'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the sentence aloud; a comma goes only where it separates list items, an opening phrase or a name being spoken to.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Misses how a comma changes the meaning
misconceptions.description: Picks 'Come and help me cook Sameer.' as the sentence where Sameer is spoken to.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read both versions aloud and picture what each one says is happening.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the opening or closing speech marks
misconceptions.description: Writes 'My kite is stuck, said Om.' or '"I found a shell, said Riya.'
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a speech mark before the first spoken word and after the last spoken word and its mark.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Ends the spoken words with a full stop before said
misconceptions.description: Writes '"We are going to the beach." said Leela.'
misconceptions.repair_hint: When said comes after the speech, end the spoken words with a comma, not a full stop.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the comma between the speech and said
misconceptions.description: Writes '"Not me" said Rohan.' or 'Mum said "Please wash your hands."'
misconceptions.repair_hint: A comma separates the spoken words from said, asked or shouted.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps two speakers on the same line
misconceptions.description: Writes Tara's question and Sam's reply on one line, one after the other.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Each time a new person speaks, start a new line.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out the apostrophe of the owner
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Riyas bag' or 'the girls hall' with no apostrophe.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: does something belong to this person? Then add an apostrophe.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts the apostrophe on the wrong side of the s
misconceptions.description: Writes 'the boy's bags' for two boys, or 'the dogs' tail' for one dog.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Write the owner word first (boy or boys), then add the apostrophe: one owner 's, many owners ending in s just '.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Adds 's to a plural that already ends in s
misconceptions.description: Writes boys's or sisters's.
misconceptions.repair_hint: If the owners already end in s, add only the apostrophe: boys'.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts an apostrophe in a plural that owns nothing
misconceptions.description: Writes 'Fresh mango's for sale' or 'two banana's'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: does the next word belong to it? If not, it is just a plural: mangoes.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Writes childrens' or childrens
misconceptions.description: Writes 'the childrens' playground' or 'the childrens playground'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Children does not end in s, so add 's: children's, men's, women's.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies or picks a fact next to the answer
misconceptions.description: Copies words that sit near the key word but answer a different question: writes "green" for the colour of Riya's kite, which is the parrot's colour.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the key word, then read the whole sentence it is in and ask: does this answer my question?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Answers from what they know, not from the passage
misconceptions.description: Picks an answer that sounds likely but the passage never says: ticks "to the park" when the story says the terrace.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a finger on the words in the passage that say it; if you cannot find them, choose again.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks the option that repeats a word from the passage, not the answer
misconceptions.description: Ticks an option because its words appear in the passage, though they do not answer the question: "to the water tank" for where Riya took her kite.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say the question again in your own words, then check that the option answers that question, not just matches a word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies a detail that does not show what was asked
misconceptions.description: Copies words about the character or place that show something else: copies "always the first to help" when asked what Kabir looked like.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: does this tell me how they look, how they act, or what the place is like? Match it to the question.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Describes a different character, thing or place
misconceptions.description: Copies words that describe something else in the passage: writes "wet" for the ground, when wet describes the jamuns.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the name of the person or place in the question, and copy only the words that belong to it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Finds the words but does not say what they show
misconceptions.description: Writes the clue only, with no meaning: "She held Amma's hand tightly." and nothing about Nisha being scared.
misconceptions.repair_hint: After the clue, add "This shows that ..." and say what the reader learns about the character or place.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Describes the character from their own idea, not the text
misconceptions.description: Gives a trait with no support in the story: "Mr Joshi is lazy", when nothing in the passage shows it.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Every word you use to describe a character needs a clue in the story; underline the clue first.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Keeps the events in the order they are printed
misconceptions.description: Numbers the events 1, 2, 3 down the page as they are printed, not in the order they happen in the story.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find each event in the passage and number them by where they come in the story, not by where they are on the paper.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Swaps two events that happen close together
misconceptions.description: Gets most of the order right but swaps two neighbours: puts "Om began to cry" before the wind blew.
misconceptions.repair_hint: For two events close together, ask: which one had to happen first for the other one to happen?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives a later event as the cause
misconceptions.description: Chooses something that happened afterwards as the reason: "She gave him four ladoos" for why Dev went to the door alone.
misconceptions.repair_hint: A cause comes before what it causes; check that your reason happened earlier in the story.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives an earlier event that did not cause it
misconceptions.description: Chooses something that happened before but is not the reason: "because the bus was yellow" for why the ride took an hour.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say it as "... so ...": "The bus was yellow, so the ride took an hour" sounds wrong; try each choice this way.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses from a word in the title, not from what the book is about
misconceptions.description: Picks the reader who wants a science book about clouds because the title has the word clouds, though the blurb says it is a magical story.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the whole blurb and say what kind of book it is before you think about the title.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses the book they would like, not the one the reader needs
misconceptions.description: Ticks the exciting adventure for a reader who is just starting chapter books and likes reading aloud.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Underline what the reader in the question likes and needs, and check the blurb against those words.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up a story book and a book of facts
misconceptions.description: Chooses the story book for a project on animals, or says a story is a book of facts.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for clue words: mystery, adventure and story mean a story; facts, photographs and how or why questions mean an information book.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives a reason with no detail from the blurb or review
misconceptions.description: Writes "because it looks good" or "because I like it" with nothing the blurb or review says.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Finish your reason with "The blurb says ..." or "The review says ..." and copy a few words.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads the page from the line above or below
misconceptions.description: Writes 9 for camels because the eye slips to the next line, cobras ... 9.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a ruler under the entry and slide your finger along the dots to its own page number.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Looks up an entry that shares a word but is not the topic
misconceptions.description: Writes the pages for rain when the question is about floods, or picks Kinds of mangoes for a recipe.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say what you want to find out in one word, then think of other words for it before you look in the list.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives only the first page when the index lists more
misconceptions.description: Writes 5 for rangoli when the index says 5, 14.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read to the end of the line: every number after the entry is a page about it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses the contents page when the index is needed, or the other way round
misconceptions.description: Says to use the contents page to find every page that mentions lanterns.
misconceptions.repair_hint: The contents page lists the chapters in page order; the index lists small topics in a-b-c order with every page.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a small detail as the main point
misconceptions.description: Ticks "Auto-rickshaws have three wheels" as what the whole passage is about.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: is every sentence about this? A main point covers most of the passage, a detail only one sentence.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes the first sentence as the main point
misconceptions.description: Ticks "The air on Vetal Hill smelled of wet earth" because it comes first.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read to the end before you decide; the main point can be in the middle or at the end.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives a main point bigger than the passage
misconceptions.description: Chooses "Every Way to Travel in the World" as the title for a passage only about auto-rickshaws.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Check the main point against the passage: does the passage really talk about all of that?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Retells every detail instead of one main point
misconceptions.description: Writes a long list: "Simran brings rajma and Joseph brings idli and Farah has a sandwich and ..."
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the passage and say in one sentence what it was about; leave out names and numbers.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads a clue only at face value
misconceptions.description: Takes what a character does or says as the whole story and misses the hint, or copies a sentence back: says Kabir 'was cold' when his ears turned pink after a lie.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: why would someone do that? What might they be feeling inside?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses one clue and ignores the rest
misconceptions.description: Picks a feeling that fits a single clue, often from another part of the story: says Arjun felt proud when he was picked last, because he was proud later on.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find every clue near that moment and check the feeling fits all of them.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Answers from own ideas, not the text
misconceptions.description: Gives a feeling or reason that no clue in the passage supports: says Riya felt excited after her kite flew away.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Point to the words in the passage that made you think that; if there are none, look again.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Retells what happened instead of the lesson
misconceptions.description: Gives an event from the story as its lesson: writes 'Anu walked to school in the rain' when asked what the story teaches.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: what should we learn from this, for our own lives?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a small detail as the big idea
misconceptions.description: Names a thing or a small part of the story as its theme: says the story is about rain or about a cricket bat, not about kindness.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: is this idea true of the whole story, from beginning to end?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Matches stories by how they look, not by their lesson
misconceptions.description: Says two stories share a theme because they have the same place or the same kind of animal: matches a story about an honest girl in a shop with any story set in a shop.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Say each story's lesson in a few words first, then compare the lessons.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Reads only one telling
misconceptions.description: Answers about one telling as if it were both: says 'the bird is a crow' is the same in both, when the second telling has a sparrow.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the first telling, then the second, and find the detail in each before you answer.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up what stays the same and what changes
misconceptions.description: Calls a change a sameness, or a sameness a change: says the endings are the same when one monkey escapes and the other makes friends again.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Put a finger on the detail in each telling and ask: are these two the same or not?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Puts a detail in the wrong telling
misconceptions.description: Writes a detail from the second telling in the box for the first: puts 'a puddle' for the dog of long ago, who sees itself in a stream.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at the heading of each telling and check which one the detail comes from.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Predicts an ending the story gives no clue for
misconceptions.description: Chooses or writes an ending that ignores what has happened: says Priya's seed will fly away after she has watered it every day.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Name one thing that has already happened, and make your ending follow from it.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Retells the story instead of predicting
misconceptions.description: Gives something that has already happened as the ending: writes 'Priya planted a seed' when asked what will happen next.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: what has not happened yet? Your ending comes after the last line.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives an ending with no reason
misconceptions.description: Writes an ending but no 'because': writes 'Farah wins' and nothing about why, from the story or from stories like it.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Add 'because' and a clue from the story, or a story you know that went the same way.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Leaves out a step
misconceptions.description: Misses a step or stops early, so the result is wrong: after 'write pan, write it backwards, put s in front, change a to i' writes spin, because the backwards step was missed.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Tick each step as you do it, and do not start the next one until the last is ticked.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Does the steps in the wrong order
misconceptions.description: Follows the steps in the order they are printed when the time words say otherwise, or runs past the step asked about: puts the sev on the bhel before the chutney.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Underline time words like before, after and just before, then number the steps.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Misreads a direction word
misconceptions.description: Follows a step but swaps a small word such as left and right, first and last, or front and end: looks under the bench on the left when the step says right.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Circle the direction words in each step and say them aloud before you act.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Calls an opinion a fact
misconceptions.description: Sorts a sentence that says what someone thinks into facts, often because it sounds sure: puts 'Our mangoes are the sweetest in the world' with the facts.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: could everyone check this and agree? Look for words like best, sweetest, lovely and should.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Calls a fact an opinion
misconceptions.description: Sorts a sentence that can be checked into opinions, often because it is about something nice: puts 'Tickets cost twenty rupees' with the opinions.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: could you check this by looking, counting or asking? If yes, it is a fact.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Misses the word that shows an opinion
misconceptions.description: Picks a naming word as the clue to an opinion instead of the feeling word: chooses 'mangoes' rather than 'sweetest' in 'Our mangoes are the sweetest in the world'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Find the word that says what someone thinks or feels; that word makes it an opinion.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes the answer from the wrong part of the text
misconceptions.description: Copies or ticks a nearby detail that does not answer the question: writes 'Every morning' when asked what time the bus comes.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Underline the key word in the question, find the sentence with that idea, and read that sentence again before answering.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Answers from a guess, not the text
misconceptions.description: Ticks or writes something the passage never says, or says the opposite of: 'Neha let go of the string' when the story says the string snapped.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: where does it say that? Put a finger on the words in the passage before choosing.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Uses only one of the two places
misconceptions.description: Gives only part of the answer when it is spread over two places: names the paper and sticks for Neha's kite but leaves out the ribbon tail.
misconceptions.repair_hint: When a question says 'two places', tick each part of the passage as you use it and check both are in the answer.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies what happens, not what shows the character
misconceptions.description: Copies an event that tells nothing about what the person is like: writes 'Raghu drives his auto-rickshaw' as words that show he is kind.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: what do these words tell me about the person? Choose words that show a feeling, a habit or a way of acting.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies words about the wrong person or quality
misconceptions.description: Copies words about a different character, a different part of the place, or a different quality from the one asked: writes 'under tall coconut trees' when asked for the sound of the rain.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the question again and name the person and the quality it asks about before looking for words.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Describes the character without the story's words
misconceptions.description: Names a quality ('Farhan is shy') but quotes no words from the story to show it.
misconceptions.repair_hint: After naming the quality, add 'because the story says …' and copy the words.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Swaps the problem and the resolution
misconceptions.description: Matches the part where things go wrong to 'Resolution', or the part where it is put right to 'Problem': calls 'a gust of wind blew across the step' the ending.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask two questions of each part: is something going wrong here, or is it being put right?

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up the opening and the build-up
misconceptions.description: Calls the part that only says who and where the build-up, or calls the first event the opening: matches 'Rohan's side batted first' to Opening.
misconceptions.repair_hint: The opening only sets the scene: who, where and when. Anything that starts to happen belongs to the build-up.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Mixes up the resolution and the ending
misconceptions.description: Calls the moment the problem is solved the ending, or the last calm scene the resolution: matches 'Grandfather took his medicine on time' to Ending.
misconceptions.repair_hint: The resolution is how the problem is solved; the ending is how things are left afterwards.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Follows the printed order, not the stages
misconceptions.description: Numbers mixed-up paragraphs in the order they are printed (A, B, C, D, E), or calls the first printed paragraph the opening or introduction even when it is not.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look for the paragraph that says what the whole text is about or sets the scene; that is the start, wherever it is printed.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks a detail instead of the main point
misconceptions.description: Chooses an example, a number or a name that supports the point: picks 'with ginger' as the key words of a passage about tulsi being useful.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: if I took these words away, would the paragraph still make its point? If yes, they are a detail.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes the first words, whatever they say
misconceptions.description: Copies the opening words of the paragraph even when the main point comes later: picks 'In April and May' for a paragraph whose point is 'Water is precious'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Read the whole paragraph, then look for the sentence the others explain; it may be at the end.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Copies everything instead of choosing
misconceptions.description: Copies a whole long sentence or the whole paragraph, details and all, when only the key words are asked for.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cross out the words that give examples or extra detail, and copy only what is left.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Takes one detail as what the whole text is about
misconceptions.description: Chooses something mentioned once as the gist: picks 'how to stop elephants' for a recount of a class trip to Shaniwar Wada.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Look at the title, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last sentence; choose the idea they all share.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Chooses a topic far wider than the text
misconceptions.description: Picks a big, general topic that the text is only a small part of: 'food in India' for a text about Mumbai's dabbawalas.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Ask: does the text tell me about all of that? Choose the answer that fits the text and no more.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Picks the choice that repeats a word from the title
misconceptions.description: Chooses an option because it shares a word with the title or first line, not because it fits the gist: 'a long walk down stone steps' for 'A walk to Nongriat'.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Skim every paragraph's first sentence before choosing; a shared word is not enough.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks content words instead of linking words
misconceptions.description: Underlines the nouns or doing words of a sentence, such as 'umbrella, rain, stool, tea', instead of the words that join one idea to the next.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Cover the word: if the sentence still tells the same thing but the join to the last idea is lost, it is a linking word.

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Gives a linking word the wrong job
misconceptions.description: Says a link adds a point when it shows a contrast or a cause: says 'However' gives another good thing about trees.
misconceptions.repair_hint: Sort links into jobs: time (then, next), adding (also, in addition), cause (because, as a result), contrast (but, however).

misconceptions.subject: ENG
misconceptions.name: Marks single words but misses linking phrases
